text:
**Scrap the Parking Mandate**

Every city has a rule that most residents have never read and almost everyone pays for: the minimum parking requirement. It says that before anyone can build an apartment, a restaurant, or a dentist's office, they must also build a set number of parking spaces. One and a half per apartment. One per 300 square feet of retail. Ten per 1,000 square feet of restaurant. Cities should repeal these rules, and the case is stronger than many people expect.

Start with where the numbers come from. Many requirements trace back to a handbook of parking generation rates, built from surveys of suburban sites with ample free parking, often measured at their busiest hour. Planners then wrote those peaks into law as the minimum for everyone. The result is a standard calibrated to the most car-dependent places imaginable and applied to downtowns, transit corridors, and walkable neighborhoods alike. Donald Shoup, the UCLA scholar who has spent decades on this subject, found that the rates often rested on remarkably thin samples. A rule that shapes the footprint of every building in a city should not rest on that.

Next, consider the cost. A surface space takes roughly 300 square feet once you count the aisles and ramps, which is more than a small studio apartment offers a person. Structured spaces are far pricier. In many American cities, a single underground space costs tens of thousands of dollars to build. That cost does not vanish. It is folded into rents and sale prices, whether or not the tenant owns a car. A household without a vehicle ends up subsidizing storage for other people's. Research on this effect suggests that mandates raise housing costs meaningfully, and that is in a country already short of homes.

The mandates also strangle small projects. A developer with a narrow lot cannot always fit the required spaces, so the building shrinks, or turns into a smaller number of larger units, or never happens. Old main streets are full of beloved buildings that could not be legally built today because they lack the required parking. Converting an old shop into a cafe can trigger a requirement that the lot cannot meet, so the storefront sits empty. Parking rules do not just add cost. They quietly veto entire categories of modest, incremental development.

Then there is what the mandates do to the shape of the city. Buildings spread apart to make room for lots. Distances grow, walking becomes less pleasant, and driving becomes the only sensible option, which in turn seems to justify more parking. It is a loop, and the law keeps it turning. Land that could hold homes, shops, or parks becomes asphalt that sits mostly empty most of the day. Cities then wonder why their centers feel hollow and their tax base per acre is low.

Defenders raise a fair worry: if cities stop requiring parking, will streets fill with cars circling for spaces? This fear mistakes repeal for prohibition. Removing a minimum does not ban a single space. It lets developers and lenders decide how much parking a project needs, and they have strong reasons to get it right. A building with too few spaces for its market will struggle to attract tenants and buyers. Developers in suburban and rural settings will keep building plenty. What changes is that the dense, transit-rich, walkable places can stop pretending they are a highway interchange.

Where parking is truly scarce, the answer is pricing, not mandates. Free curb parking invites overuse; a modest, well-managed fee, ideally with the revenue returned to the neighborhood, keeps a few spaces open and eliminates much of the cruising. That tool is far more precise than a blanket requirement stamped on every building.

The evidence from places that have tried repeal is encouraging. Buffalo eliminated its citywide minimums in 2017, and others, including Minneapolis, Anchorage, and many smaller cities, have followed. These cities did not descend into gridlock. Builders there often still provide parking where the market wants it, but they now have room to build homes, shrink footprints, and respond to actual demand rather than a formula. Reform has also been easier to pass than many expected, because the rule is so hard to defend once someone asks why it exists.

There is a fairness argument too. Roughly one in ten American households has no car at all, and the share is far higher among lower-income renters in big cities. Parking mandates ask the people with the least to pay for something they do not use. Repeal returns that choice to the household. Those who want a space can buy or rent one. Those who do not are no longer charged for it.

Finally, the climate and budget case lines up with the housing case. Compact, walkable neighborhoods mean fewer miles driven and cheaper infrastructure per household. Cities spend enormous sums maintaining roads and utilities that serve sprawling, low-density patterns. Parking minimums are one of the quiet mechanisms that produce them.

None of this means cars are bad or that parking has no place. It means a city council should not be deciding, in advance and for every lot in town, how much of the ground must be dedicated to storing vehicles. That decision belongs to the people building and using the property, with the city setting fair prices for the public street. Repeal the mandate, price the curb, and let neighborhoods grow into whatever they are meant to be.
